title: When God Commanded Violence—What It Really Means (Joshua 6:21)
paragraphs: When God Commanded Violence—What It Really Means (Joshua 6:21)

He didn’t whisper mercy there.
He ordered destruction.
That’s the part many people want to skip in Joshua 6:21.
“And they devoted all in the city to destruction…” Joshua 6:21.
Hard verse. Heavy verse. A verse that can make even sincere believers pause and ask, Why would a holy God command violence?
Here’s what it really means.

First, Jericho was not a random victim of divine anger. This was not God losing control. This was judgment. Long-delayed judgment. The people of Canaan had filled up generations of rebellion, idolatry, and wickedness, and God had been patient far longer than we would have been. Scripture shows that this moment did not come suddenly. It came after centuries of mercy ignored.

Second, the destruction of Jericho was tied to something sacred and severe: God’s justice against sin. We like the God who heals. We like the God who restores. Amen. But He is also the God who judges evil. If God never judges sin, then He is not holy. He is not righteous. He is not God.
But here’s what we miss.
Joshua 6 is not mainly about God being cruel. It is about God being uncompromisingly holy.
And that should shake us.

Because the real scandal is not that God judged Jericho.
The real scandal is that He has not destroyed all of us.

We read Joshua 6 and ask, “How could God do that to them?”
The Gospel turns the question around: “Why has God shown mercy to me?”
And that’s where grace walks in.

In the same Jericho story, Rahab was spared. A woman with a broken past. A woman marked by shame. Yet she believed the God of Israel, and mercy found her in the middle of judgment. That is the signpost. Even in a chapter of destruction, God was already preaching salvation.
Rahab points forward to Jesus.

Because at the cross, God’s justice and God’s mercy collided without contradiction. Sin was judged. Not ignored. Judged. But the judgment fell on Christ for all who believe. The wrath we fear, Jesus absorbed. The mercy we do not deserve, Jesus gives.
So what does Joshua 6:21 really mean?

It means God is serious about sin.
It means judgment is real.
It means holiness is not soft.
And it means mercy is astonishing.
Read Jericho, then look at Calvary.

One city fell under judgment.
One Savior stood under judgment.
That is the difference.

So do not read this passage like an outsider examining God from a distance. Read it like a sinner standing in desperate need of grace. Because the same Bible that shows walls falling also shows a cross standing.
And at that cross, there is hope for the guilty.
Even now.
Even for you.

Prayer:
Lord, help us not to shrink Your holiness or sentimentalize Your mercy. Teach us to tremble at sin and run to Christ. Thank You that in Jesus, judgment is not the end of the story for those who repent and believe. Amen.
